newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-Guitarist McLaughlin looks back for ideas.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Guitarist McLaughlin looks back for ideas.

text.p: Guitarist John McLaughlin has made a full-time job lately of revisiting the musical ideas that made him famous as one of the most eclectic and revered risk-takers in jazz.

But McLaughlin, one of the pioneers of the jazz-rock fusion movement in the 1960s and 1970s and a leading proponent of "world music" before the term was coined, is not aiming to relive past success. Instead, he is mining musical ideals that were far from exhausted the first time around.

"We change and evolve. This is a permanent factor in life and our musical conceptions also evolve with that," he said in a telephone interview from San Diego in the midst of a North American tour with his newly reunited accoustic guitar trio. "I suppose it must be similar to a painter who will adopt a concept in his painting and explore that, but that will, in turn, lead him onto another way of articulating what he is trying to say."

The Guitar Trio, which also includes fellow fusion star Al Di Meola and flamenco guitar great Paco de Lucia, is an example of how the British-born guitar legend is dabbing in familiar colors on his palette. The group, which melds intricate flamenco, jazz and classical guitar styles, made waves with its debut live recording "Friday Night In San Francisco" in 1981. But 14 years passed before the guitarists joined forces again.

The Guitar Trio's current tour and a new studio album came after McLaughlin invited de Lucia and Di Meola to appear on "The Promise," a CD that featured such other past collaborators as organist/trumpeter Joey DeFrancesco, percussionist Trilok Gurtu and drummer Dennis Chambers.

The trio shares an artistic chemistry and an appreciation of the challenging mix of styles. "They're both leaders in their own right," he said of his collaborators. "They're playing my instrument, which is a good enough reason to hate them. But it's very challenging musically because there are no drums, no bass, no percussion, no keyboards -- you're very exposed."

The result is a mix of guitar precision and subtlety that produces at various times stunning flurries of notes and quiet, sultry passages. Their music is a stark contrast to the blistering electric guitar sound that made McLaughlin a household name in jazz circles as a part of Miles Davis' fusion groups in the late 1960s and leader of fusion's first supergroup, Mahavishnu Orchestra, in the early 1970s.

McLaughlin said he tried until about 10 years ago to reunite the original Mahavishnu, which included such players as keyboardist Jan Hammer and drummer Billy Cobham, but personality clashes made it impossible.

"I would have loved to get that together because the original group existed only for two years, which is really a short time," he said. "I think we had maybe too much success commercially speaking. There's a lot more music that could have been played and worked out."

The group's name was revived for two recordings in the mid-1980s with different players and middling results. But McLaughlin plans to revisit some jazz-rock ideas with a new group next year. He also aims to bring together musicians to perform Indian-flavored music such as that from another of his 1970s groups, Shakti.

Interest in jazz-rock fusion, with its long guitar and keyboard solos and complex rhythms, nearly died altogether in the early 1980s after being roundly disparaged by a new group of musicians aiming to return to the mainstream jazz sounds that existed in the 1950s. But 16 years later, he said, many of the ideas that were pioneered by McLaughlin and his cohorts are being rediscovered in the "acid jazz" scene, which merges jazz, rock and funk styles in an often frenetic package.

"It's all cyclical in the end. This acid jazz movement a lot of people mock also but I think this is an era. I think a lot of great things have already come out of acid jazz and will continue to do so."
